title: A co-tenant workload steals host CPU: services wait on the runqueue, not on I/O

problem.summary: An unrelated workload sharing the host consumes CPU. Application services are never themselves busy, but each time they become ready to run they wait measurably longer before a CPU actually runs them. User-facing latency moves only slightly, so dashboards look nearly normal; the delay is only visible in the scheduler.
symptoms: mild, intermittent latency jitter across several unrelated services at once
no service is itself busy: per-container CPU is flat or falling
no new error signatures; requests still succeed
host CPU busy rises but is not exhausted, and host load rises moderately

discriminators.signal: host CPU utilisation during the incident, computed from sched_switch on-CPU time
discriminators.this_problem: utilisation rises but keeps real headroom - the host is being shared, not exhausted
discriminators.not_this_problem: utilisation reaches the ceiling (host exhaustion), FALLS below baseline (a cgroup quota holding work back), or stays flat (healthy)
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED on 17 labelled runs across four families. Co-tenant 0.619-0.681 (n=5); host saturation 0.991-0.998 (n=3); no-fault 0.462-0.531 (n=5); cgroup cap 0.114-0.365 (n=4). Baseline was 0.444-0.507 in all 17 runs. The automated overlap check reports a clean split. See evidence/cpu_cluster_separation.json

discriminators.signal: cores gained by a process that consumed no CPU in the baseline window
discriminators.this_problem: a newcomer takes a bounded amount - measured 0.99 to 2.00 cores on a 12-CPU host
discriminators.not_this_problem: the newcomer takes several cores and pins the host (host exhaustion), or there is no newcomer at all (cgroup quota, healthy)
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED: co-tenant newcomer gained 0.988-2.002 cores (n=5, present 5/5) against 6.544-6.624 for host saturation (n=3) and 0.000-0.296 for no-fault runs (1/5 had any newcomer). The measurement recovers the recipe's own cgroup cap to within 1% (CPUS=1.0 -> 0.988/0.997; CPUS=2.0 -> 1.978/1.978/2.002), which is why we trust the attribution. NOTE: the newcomer has the SAME process name as in host saturation, because they are the same mechanism at different intensities - identity never separates them. See evidence/cpu_cluster_separation.json

discriminators.signal: blocking duration of socket-WAITING syscalls (poll, epoll_wait, recvfrom, read, select)
discriminators.this_problem: socket-waiting durations stay flat: nothing is blocking longer, the threads simply cannot get a CPU
discriminators.not_this_problem: one component's socket-waiting syscall inflates by an order of magnitude
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED on 5 co-tenant runs: max socket-waiting inflation is 1.5-2.99x, versus 36.83x for the datastore fault. IMPORTANT refinement found while testing: general syscalls DO lengthen under CPU starvation because the thread is descheduled inside them - connect() reached 5.3x - so only socket-WAITING calls may be used to rule this problem out. See evidence/L0_blocking_syscall_CONTROL_cotenant.json and the 5-run comparison.

discriminators.this_problem: no component has slow incoming edges; the slowdown does not converge anywhere
discriminators.not_this_problem: slow edges converge on one component
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED: edge_convergence.py returns converged_on = null on the co-tenant run, max edge slowdown 1.7x with zero edges over the 2x threshold. See evidence/L0_edge_convergence_CONTROL_cotenant.json

discriminators.this_problem: a container consumes steady CPU it did not consume in the baseline and has NO call-graph edges
discriminators.not_this_problem: the extra CPU belongs to a service that appears in the call graph
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED: the co-tenant consumed 2.00 cores against a 0.00 baseline with no call-path edges; host busy cores 5.31 -> 7.96 (x1.5), so the host retained headroom. See evidence/measured_verdict_noisy_neighbor_r1.json

discriminators.signal: runqueue delay: time from sched_waking to the sched_switch that runs the thread
discriminators.this_problem: raised - measured 7.12x - but this is CORROBORATION, not evidence. It must never be the deciding signal
discriminators.not_this_problem: runqueue delay alone separates nothing: it is raised in every CPU-family fault and in healthy load bursts too, and its ordering is inverted against severity
discriminators.evidence: MEASURED across the negative-class sweep: host saturation 36.97-52.54x, cgroup cap 13.54-15.70x, THIS fault 7.12x, healthy burst 3.69x. Using it as the positive test produced a 42% false-positive rate and diagnosed a healthy system as this fault at 0.80 confidence. See docs/FINDINGS-phase1.md findings F1-F3.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: the delayed services show a raised runnable_wait share (ready to run, waiting for a CPU)
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: runnable_wait of the labelled culprit never exceeds 4% in ANY fault family (max 4.0% svc_mem_cap, 2.6% the cgroup-cap family); on the co-tenant run the highest runnable_wait across services was 1.6%. See evidence/wait_signature_all_families.json
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: removed from the discriminators. Do not reinstate without new evidence.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: The share of wall time a service spends in a runnable state. Measured across every labelled fault: it never exceeds 4%, because that share is diluted by ordinary idle waiting. Use per-wakeup runqueue DELAY instead, which shows the effect clearly.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: the wait decomposition of the culprit distinguishes this fault
unverified_do_not_claim.status: CANNOT BE MEASURED for this family
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: this fault is labelled against the host, and L2 produces no record for 'host'. Across 93 runs there is no culprit-side L2 record for the host-saturation family, anomaly_disk, anomaly_mem, anomaly_net or the co-tenant family.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: either derive a host-level L2 record, or accept that this family is diagnosed from metrics + topology only.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: The wait decomposition of the culprit. For host-attributed faults no culprit-side wait record exists at all, so its absence is meaningless here.

unverified_do_not_claim.claim: broadly inflated runqueue delay identifies co-tenant CPU contention
unverified_do_not_claim.status: NOT SUPPORTED - the signal is present in every neighbouring fault and in healthy bursts
unverified_do_not_claim.measurement: Runqueue delay was raised in all four CPU-cluster families (52.54x host saturation, 15.70x cgroup cap, 7.12x this fault, 3.69x a healthy burst). Deciding on it gave 5 false fires in 12 negative runs, including normal_none_burst_r1 - a healthy system - reported as this fault at 0.80 confidence.
unverified_do_not_claim.consequence: demoted to corroboration. The deciding signal is host utilisation with headroom plus a bounded newcomer.
unverified_do_not_claim.agent_note: How long ready threads waited for a CPU. It rises under every kind of CPU trouble and under ordinary load bursts, so on its own it tells you the machine is loaded, not what is wrong.

reproduction.system: Sock Shop or Train Ticket on Ubuntu 24.04, LTTng 2.15, Docker 27+, single GCP n2 VM

traces: server span duration per service, only to confirm the impact is mild
collection_order.why_these: MEASURED BASIS. Runqueue delay needs exactly two tracepoints: sched_waking gives the moment a thread became runnable, and sched_switch (next_tid) gives the moment a CPU actually ran it. The difference is the delay. Syscall events are collected only as the NEGATIVE control - showing durations stay flat is what separates this from a component blocked on I/O. Nothing else in the kernel trace is required.

processing.expect: a CTF directory with metadata and channel streams

processing.step: attribute on-CPU time per process, baseline window against incident window
processing.expect: host utilisation raised but below the ceiling, and one newcomer holding 1-2 cores

processing.step: Measure runqueue delay per process, baseline vs incident
processing.expect: a broad multi-process inflation of p95 indicates contention

processing.step: NEGATIVE CONTROL: confirm blocking-syscall durations did not inflate
processing.expect: no syscall inflates much; a large single-component inflation means this is the wrong blueprint

processing.step: Identify the off-call-path CPU consumer and emit the verdict
processing.expect: the top CPU consumer has no call-graph edges and was absent in the baseline

processing.step: State the recommended action alongside the diagnosis
processing.expect: a concrete action naming the container to constrain, not a generic suggestion

outputs.contains: culprit container, per-service runnable-wait share baseline versus incident, host CPU headroom
runnable-wait share per service over time, with the incident window shaded
which container took the CPU, which services waited, and why this is contention rather than saturation
what to do about it: identify and reschedule or cap the co-tenant workload, or move the affected services to a less contended host

verdict_when: host CPU utilisation rises during the incident but retains clear headroom
a process that consumed no CPU in the baseline now holds a bounded one to two cores
that process has no role in the call graph
runqueue delay is broadly inflated, corroborating that ready threads are queueing

rule_out.when: utilisation reaches the ceiling and the newcomer takes several cores - the host is exhausted, not shared
utilisation FALLS below baseline and there is no newcomer - a quota is holding work back
utilisation is flat and no newcomer took meaningful CPU, even if a load burst raised runqueue delay

rule_out.instead: a component waiting on I/O or a dependency
rule_out.when: one component's blocking syscall inflates by an order of magnitude while runqueue delay stays flat
host CPU is exhausted rather than merely raised, and user latency collapses instead of jittering

rule_out.instead: a service pinned by its own CPU limit
rule_out.when: only ONE service is delayed and it is on the call path

decision.root_cause_is: the co-tenant workload container itself, not any application service it delays

evidence_from_literature.claim: Runqueue delay separates CPU starvation from self-inflicted slowness better than utilisation does
evidence_from_literature.validated_on: our labelled co-tenant runs on both applications

provenance.notes: v3: rebuilt on the raw kernel trace read with babeltrace2, after the derived wait-share record was measured to be non-discriminative. Every discriminator now cites a measurement with its control. The decisive pair: runqueue delay 7.12x here vs 0.97x on the datastore fault, and the datastore's poll syscall 1.12x here vs 36.83x there - same signals, opposite directions. v6: discriminator narrowed from 'syscall durations' to 'socket-waiting syscall durations' after 5-run testing showed connect() inflating 5.3x under CPU starvation and wrongly vetoing the verdict on 2 of 5 runs. v7 (2026-08-29): rewritten after the CPU-cluster measurement. Runqueue delay demoted from deciding signal to corroboration after it was measured raised in every neighbouring fault and in healthy bursts; host utilisation with headroom plus a bounded newcomer is now the discriminator. The container-attribution step moved from metrics to the kernel trace. v8 (2026-08-29): added measured scenarios from the two-application re-test. The same fault produces different signatures on a short call chain and on a wide fan-out system; both are recorded rather than averaged into one threshold, because the point of a blueprint is to tell someone what to expect and where to look, not to be one tuned number.

taxonomy.note: A blueprint covers this whole subcategory, not one incident. It was authored from labelled co-tenant runs but is written to apply to any case where ready threads cannot get a CPU.

apply_when: several unrelated services degrade mildly at the same time
error rates are unchanged and requests still succeed
do_not_apply_when: one component alone is slow while the rest are healthy
requests are failing or timing out rather than merely slowing
the host is fully exhausted and latency collapses rather than jitters
applicability.cheap_precheck: host CPU rose but retains headroom, and no container on the call graph accounts for the extra CPU

capabilities_required.why: the stored kernel trace must be readable
the decisive signal: how long ready threads waited for a CPU
negative control: showing syscall durations stayed flat rules out I/O waiting
the deciding signal: host utilisation with headroom, and the bounded newcomer that took the CPU. Previously sourced from metrics; measured to be recoverable from the scheduler stream alone

stopping_conditions.conclude: runqueue delay is broadly inflated, syscall durations are flat, and an off-call-path container accounts for the CPU
stopping_conditions.stop_and_switch: a single component's blocking syscall inflates by an order of magnitude while runqueue delay stays flat -> use the dependency-wait blueprint
stopping_conditions.stop_insufficient: runqueue delay cannot be computed because the scheduler events were not recorded -> request them and re-run; do not guess from utilisation alone

adaptation_rules.if: the runqueue signal is present but no off-call-path container is found
adaptation_rules.then: the contention is internal: re-check whether an on-call-path service is consuming the CPU, which points at a service-level cause instead

adaptation_rules.if: only one process shows inflated runqueue delay
adaptation_rules.then: this is not host-wide contention; consider a per-service CPU limit

adaptation_rules.if: the trace covers less than the full incident window
adaptation_rules.then: widen the window before comparing, since short windows exaggerate percentiles

preconditions: kernel scheduler events are collectable or already collected

historical_effectiveness.note: 5 labelled co-tenant runs at two intensities, separated from 12 runs of three neighbouring families with no overlap on the deciding signal. Sock Shop only; Train Ticket owed.

policies.collection_order_rule: Use evidence that already exists before enabling any new collection. Escalate a tier only when the cheaper tier leaves a candidate cause unresolved, and record why.

scope.restrict_to: the hosts and time window named in the intent

privacy: do not retain personally identifiable data
preserve request identifiers only where permitted

requires_approval: widening the host scope or time window

policies.autonomy_note: Level 2 = policy-controlled automation: select and execute low-risk plans inside the stated constraints. Level 3 (adaptive escalation within the allowed action space) is the next target; closed-loop remediation is explicitly out of scope.

evidence_sufficiency.if_below_floor: name the unresolved question, pick the ONE additional capability that would settle it, check it against the overhead budget, and request it. Do not broaden collection generally.
evidence_sufficiency.report_when_stuck: if the floor is still not met after the allowed rounds, report the best-supported hypothesis, its confidence, and precisely what evidence is missing - never present a guess as a diagnosis

scenarios.note: SCENARIOS record how this problem looks on different system shapes. They are measured, not assumed, and both pictures matter: a blueprint carrying only one application's numbers would mislead anyone running the other kind of system.

cases.recognise_by: the system normally runs around half its CPU capacity
cases.what_you_see: the newcomer pushes utilisation up clearly and visibly. Measured: 0.48 baseline rising to 0.62-0.68.
cases.confidence: high - both the newcomer and the utilisation rise are obvious

cases.recognise_by: the system normally runs at 80% CPU or more
cases.what_you_see: the newcomer takes the SAME cores, but utilisation barely moves. Measured: 0.80 baseline rising only to 0.81-0.85, a change of 0.03-0.06. A percentage-based rule will miss this entirely.
cases.confidence: high IF you rank on the newcomer's cores rather than on utilisation
cases.do_this_instead: identify the fault by the absolute cores the newcomer took, and use utilisation only to check whether the host still had room. Measured across both systems the newcomer took 0.99-2.00 cores in every single run, because that number is set by the intruding workload rather than by the application.
